This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)

* [Lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon"): 1,624 craters (31.2%)
* Venusian: 900 craters (17.3%)
* [Mercurian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mercury "List of craters on Mercury"): 397 craters (7.6%)
* [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars"): 1,092 craters (21.0%)
* Others: 1,198 craters (23.0%)

Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017.[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-5)

This is a list of [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus "Venus"), [named](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union")'s (IAU) [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"). All craters on Venus are named after famous women or female first names.[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-6) *(For features on Venus other than craters see, [list of montes on Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_montes_on_Venus "List of montes on Venus") and [List of coronae on Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_coronae_on_Venus "List of coronae on Venus").[[6]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Target-Venus-7))*

As of 2017, there are 900 named craters on Venus,[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1) fewer than the [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon") and [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") craters but more than [on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mercury "List of craters on Mercury").[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-5)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)

* [Lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon"): 1,624 craters (31.2%)
* Venusian: 900 craters (17.3%)
* [Mercurian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mercury "List of craters on Mercury"): 397 craters (7.6%)
* [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars"): 1,092 craters (21.0%)
* Others: 1,198 craters (23.0%)

Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017.[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-5)

This is a list of [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus "Venus"), [named](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union")'s (IAU) [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"). All craters on Venus are named after famous women or female first names.[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-6) *(For features on Venus other than craters see, [list of montes on Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_montes_on_Venus "List of montes on Venus") and [List of coronae on Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_coronae_on_Venus "List of coronae on Venus").[[6]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Target-Venus-7))*

As of 2017, there are 900 named craters on Venus,[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1) fewer than the [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon") and [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") craters but more than [on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mercury "List of craters on Mercury").[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-5)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame

The [Rock and Roll Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_Roll_Hall_of_Fame "Rock and Roll Hall of Fame"), established in 1983 and located in [Cleveland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland "Cleveland"), [Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio "Ohio"), United States, is dedicated to recording the history of some of the best-known and most influential musicians, bands, producers, and others that have in some major way influenced the music industry, particularly in the area of [rock and roll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_roll "Rock and roll").[[1]](#cite_note-1) Originally, there were four categories of induction: [performers](#Performers), [non-performers](#Non-performers_(Ahmet_Ertegun_Award)), [early influences](#Musical_influence), and [lifetime achievement](#Lifetime_achievement). In 2000, sidemen was introduced as a category, which has since been altered to [musical excellence](#Award_for_Musical_Excellence).

The only category that has seen new inductees every single year is the performers category. Artists become eligible for induction in that category 25 years after the release of their first record.[[2]](#cite_note-Induction-2) In order to be inducted, an artist must be nominated by a committee that selects a number of candidates. [Ballots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballot "Ballot") are then sent to more than 1,000 "rock experts" who evaluate the candidates and vote on who should be inducted. The performers that receive the highest number of votes are inducted. This number varies; for example, seven were inducted in 2019. Starting in 2012, fans could vote on a fan ballot with an equal weight to the other ballots.[[2]](#cite_note-Induction-2) New inductees are honored at an annual ceremony held at the Hall of Fame in Cleveland every even-numbered year and either New York City or Los Angeles every odd-numbered year.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

The three other categories are selected by committees instead of the annual ballot.[[4]](#cite_note-vulture1-4) In 2025, Rock Hall chairman John Sykes said, "No matter what category you're in, Performer or those other three, it's the same size plaque on the wall right next to [Bob Dylan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Dylan "Bob Dylan"), [Aretha Franklin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aretha_Franklin "Aretha Franklin"), and [the Beatles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beatles "The Beatles"). It's not a secondary award. It's equal to getting in as a performer."[[4]](#cite_note-vulture1-4)

![A. P., Maybelle, and Sara Carter (L–R) in 1927](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/Carter_Family_1927.jpg/250px-Carter_Family_1927.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)

**The Carter Family** was an [American folk music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_folk_music "American folk music") group that recorded and performed between 1927 and 1956. Regarded as one of the most important music acts of the early 20th century, they had a profound influence on the development of [bluegrass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bluegrass_music "Bluegrass music"), [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music"), [southern gospel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Gospel "Southern Gospel"), [pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_music "Popular music"), and [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music"), as well as the [American folk revival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_folk_music_revival "American folk music revival") in the 1960s.

They were the first vocal group to become country music stars, and were among the first groups to record commercially produced country music. Their first recordings were made in [Bristol, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol,_Tennessee "Bristol, Tennessee"), for the [Victor Talking Machine Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Talking_Machine_Company "Victor Talking Machine Company") under producer [Ralph Peer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Peer "Ralph Peer") on August 1, 1927. This was the day before country singer [Jimmie Rodgers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmie_Rodgers_(country_singer) "Jimmie Rodgers (country singer)") made his initial recordings for Victor under Peer.

The original group consisted of [Sara Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sara_Carter "Sara Carter"), her husband [A. P. Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A._P._Carter "A. P. Carter"), and her sister-in-law [Maybelle Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maybelle_Carter "Maybelle Carter"). Maybelle was Sara's first cousin, and was married to A. P.'s brother [Ezra Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ezra_Carter "Ezra Carter") (Eck). All three were born and raised in [southwest Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwest_Virginia "Southwest Virginia"). They were immersed in the tight harmonies of mountain [gospel music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_music "Gospel music") and [shape note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shape_note "Shape note") singing. The latter dated to the early 19th century and revivals in the South.

Throughout the group's career, Sara Carter sang lead vocals and played rhythm guitar or [autoharp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autoharp "Autoharp"). Maybelle sang harmony and played lead guitar. On some songs A. P. did not perform at all; on some songs he sang harmony and background vocals, and occasionally he sang lead. Maybelle's distinctive guitar-playing style became a hallmark of the group. Her [Carter Scratch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carter_Family_picking "Carter Family picking") (a method for playing both lead and rhythm on the guitar) has become one of the most copied styles of guitar playing.

The success of the Carter Family's recordings of songs such as "[Can the Circle Be Unbroken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Can_the_Circle_Be_Unbroken_(By_and_By) "Can the Circle Be Unbroken (By and By)")", "[Wildwood Flower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wildwood_Flower "Wildwood Flower")", and "[Keep on the Sunny Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keep_on_the_Sunny_Side "Keep on the Sunny Side")" made these songs country standards that were later inducted into the [Grammy Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Hall_of_Fame "Grammy Hall of Fame"). The Carter Family was inducted in 2005 after having been the first group inducted into the [Country Music Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_Music_Hall_of_Fame_and_Museum "Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum") in 1970. The group (in all its incarnations) recorded for a number of labels, including RCA Victor (and subsidiary label, Bluebird), ARC group, Columbia, [Okeh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okeh_Records "Okeh Records") and various imprint labels.

## History

![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cf/Birthplace_log_cabin_of_A.P._Carter_at_the_Carter_Fold_at_Maces_Springs%2C_Virginia_now_Hiltons%2C_Virginia.jpg/250px-Birthplace_log_cabin_of_A.P._Carter_at_the_Carter_Fold_at_Maces_Springs%2C_Virginia_now_Hiltons%2C_Virginia.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)

The Carter Family made their first recordings on August 1, 1927.[[1]](#cite_note-Carter_Clifton-1) The previous day, [A.P. Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A._P._Carter "A. P. Carter") had persuaded his wife [Sara Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sara_Carter "Sara Carter") and his sister-in-law [Maybelle Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maybelle_Carter "Maybelle Carter") to make the short 24-mile trip from [Maces Spring, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maces_Spring,_Virginia "Maces Spring, Virginia"), to [Bristol, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol,_Tennessee "Bristol, Tennessee"), to audition for record producer [Ralph Peer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Peer "Ralph Peer"). Peer was seeking new talent for the relatively embryonic recording industry. The initial sessions are part of what are now called the [Bristol Sessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_Sessions "Bristol Sessions"), which took place the empty second floor warehouse of the Taylor-Christian hat company.[[2]](#cite_note-2) The band received $50 for each song recorded, plus a half-cent royalty on every copy sold of each song for which they had registered a copyright. On November 4, 1927, the [Victor Talking Machine Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Talking_Machine_Company "Victor Talking Machine Company") (later [RCA Victor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Victor "RCA Victor")) released a double-sided [78 rpm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/78_rpm "78 rpm") record of the group performing "Wandering Boy" and "Poor Orphan Child". On December 2, 1928, Victor released "The Storms Are on the Ocean" / "[Single Girl, Married Girl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_Girl,_Married_Girl "Single Girl, Married Girl")", which became very popular.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

By the end of 1930, the Carter Family had sold 300,000 records in the United States. Realizing that he would benefit financially with each new song he collected and [copyrighted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copyright "Copyright"), A.P. traveled around southwestern Virginia to find songs to record; he also composed new songs. In the early 1930s, he befriended [Lesley "Esley" Riddle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lesley_Riddle "Lesley Riddle"), a black guitar player from [Kingsport, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingsport,_Tennessee "Kingsport, Tennessee"). Lesley accompanied A.P. on his song-collecting trips. In June 1931, the Carters did a recording session in [Benton, Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benton,_Kentucky "Benton, Kentucky"), along with [Jimmie Rodgers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmie_Rodgers_(country_singer) "Jimmie Rodgers (country singer)"). In 1933, Maybelle met the [Speer Family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speer_Family "Speer Family") at a fair in [Ceredo, West Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceredo,_West_Virginia "Ceredo, West Virginia"), fell in love with their signature sound, and asked them to tour with the Carter Family.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

## Second generation

![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/A.P._Carter_General_Store_Museum_at_the_Carter_Fold_at_Maces_Springs%2C_Virginia_now_Hiltons%2C_Virginia.jpg/250px-A.P._Carter_General_Store_Museum_at_the_Carter_Fold_at_Maces_Springs%2C_Virginia_now_Hiltons%2C_Virginia.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)

The family spent time in their final years from 1938-1941 in [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas"), where they had a twice-daily program on the [border radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Border_blaster "Border blaster") station [XERA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XERA_(Villa_Acuña) "XERA (Villa Acuña)") (later [XERF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XERF "XERF")) in Villa Acuña (now [Ciudad Acuña, Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ciudad_Acuña "Ciudad Acuña")), across the border from [Del Rio, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Del_Rio,_Texas "Del Rio, Texas").[[3]](#cite_note-3)

In the 1939–40 season, the children of A.P. and Sara ([Janette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Janette_Carter "Janette Carter") and [Joe Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Dougherty_Carter "Joseph Dougherty Carter")) and those of Maybelle ([Helen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helen_Carter "Helen Carter"), [June](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/June_Carter_Cash "June Carter Cash"), and [Anita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anita_Carter "Anita Carter")) joined the group for radio performances, by then in [San Antonio, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Antonio,_Texas "San Antonio, Texas"). Here the programs were prerecorded and distributed to multiple border radio stations. (The children did not, however, perform on the group's records.) In the fall of 1942, the Carters moved their program to [WBT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WBT_(AM) "WBT (AM)") radio in [Charlotte, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte,_North_Carolina "Charlotte, North Carolina"), for a one-year contract. They occupied the sunrise slot, with the program airing between 5:15 and 6:15 a.m.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

Sara divorced A.P. in 1939.[[4]](#cite_note-4) After Sara married A.P.'s cousin, Coy Bayes, they moved to [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"). The Carter Family disbanded in 1944.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

Maybelle continued to perform with her daughters [Anita Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anita_Carter "Anita Carter"), [June Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/June_Carter "June Carter"), and [Helen Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helen_Carter "Helen Carter") and recorded on 3 labels (RCA Victor, Columbia and Coronet) as "[The Carter Sisters and Mother Maybelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Carter_Sisters "The Carter Sisters")" (sometimes billed as "The Carter Sisters" or "Maybelle Carter and the Carter Sisters" or "Mother Maybelle and the Carter Sisters"). In 1943, Maybelle Carter and her daughters, using the name "the Carter Sisters and Mother Maybelle" had a program on [WRNL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WRNL "WRNL") in [Richmond, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richmond,_Virginia "Richmond, Virginia").[[5]](#cite_note-5) Maybelle's brother, Hugh Jack (Doc) Addington Jr., and Carl McConnell, known as the Original Virginia Boys, also played music and sang on the radio show.

[Chet Atkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chet_Atkins "Chet Atkins"), playing electric guitar, joined them in 1949 at [WNOX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WNML_(AM)#WNOX "WNML (AM)") radio in [Knoxville, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knoxville,_Tennessee "Knoxville, Tennessee"). He moved with them in October 1949 to [KWTO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KWTO_(AM) "KWTO (AM)") radio in [Springfield, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Springfield,_Missouri "Springfield, Missouri").[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] When the Carters were offered a regular spot on the [Grand Ole Opry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Ole_Opry "Grand Ole Opry"), the Opry management did not want to include Atkins. However, Ezra Carter, their father and manager, insisted that Atkins come with them, as he was a part of their band now. Finally, the Opry management agreed, and Atkins went with them when they were hired by [WSM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WSM_(AM) "WSM (AM)") and the Grand Ole Opry; their first day was May 29, 1950. Atkins worked with them when they did "personals" off and on for 8 years, but mostly on the live Grand Ole Opry performances.[[6]](#cite_note-Atkins_Neely-6)
A.P., Sara, and their children Joe and Janette recorded 3 albums in the 1950s under the name of The A.P. Carter Family.

After the death of A.P. Carter in 1960, Mother Maybelle Carter and the Carter Sisters began using the name "the Carter Family" for their act during the 1960s and 1970s. Maybelle and Sara briefly reunited, recorded a reunion album (*An Historic Reunion*), and toured in the 1960s during the height of [folk music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music "Folk music")'s popularity.[[7]](#cite_note-YT_Sara&Maybelle_video-7)[*[non-primary source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:No_original_research#Primary,_secondary_and_tertiary_sources "Wikipedia:No original research")*]

A film documentary about the family, and in particular the second generation, *[Sunny Side of Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunny_Side_of_Life "Sunny Side of Life")*, was released in 1985.[[8]](#cite_note-8)[[9]](#cite_note-9)

In 1987, reunited sisters June Carter Cash and Helen and Anita Carter, along with June's daughter [Carlene Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlene_Carter "Carlene Carter"), appeared as the Carter Family. They were featured on a 1987 television episode of *[Austin City Limits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_City_Limits "Austin City Limits")*, along with June's husband [Johnny Cash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Cash "Johnny Cash").[[10]](#cite_note-AustinCityLimits-10)

## Third generation

The Carter Family name was revived for a third time,[*[when?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")*] under the name **Carter Family III**. It was a project of descendants of the original Carter Family, [John Carter Cash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carter_Cash "John Carter Cash") (grandson of Maybelle Carter, son of June Carter Cash and Johnny Cash) and Dale Jett (grandson of A.P. and Sara Carter), along with John's wife [Laura (Weber) Cash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laura_Weber_White "Laura Weber White"). They released their first album, *Past & Present*, in 2010.[[11]](#cite_note-11)[*[non-primary source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:No_original_research#Primary,_secondary_and_tertiary_sources "Wikipedia:No original research")*]

[Rosie Nix Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosie_Nix_Adams "Rosie Nix Adams"), daughter of June Carter Cash, performed with the Carter Family in the 1970s as well as on [The Johnny Cash Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Johnny_Cash_Show "The Johnny Cash Show") in 1969.[[12]](#cite_note-:0-12)

[Carlene Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlene_Carter "Carlene Carter") (granddaughter of Maybelle Carter) has had a successful career in country and rock music.[[12]](#cite_note-:0-12) She joined the 1987 Carter Family's second generation revival.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

**Billie Holiday** (born **Eleanora Fagan**; April 7, 1915 – July 17, 1959) was an American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") and [swing music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing_music "Swing music") singer. Nicknamed "**Lady Day**" by her friend and music partner, [Lester Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lester_Young "Lester Young"), Holiday made significant contributions to jazz music and [pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music") singing. Her vocal style, strongly influenced by jazz instrumentalists, inspired a new way of manipulating [phrasing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phrase_(music) "Phrase (music)") and [tempo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tempo "Tempo"). Holiday was known for her vocal delivery and [improvisational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_improvisation "Jazz improvisation") skills.[[1]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOstendorf,_May1993201–202-1)

After a turbulent childhood, Holiday began singing in nightclubs in [Harlem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlem "Harlem") where she was heard by producer [John Hammond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Henry_Hammond "John Henry Hammond"), who liked her voice. Holiday signed a recording contract with [Brunswick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunswick_Records "Brunswick Records") in 1935. Her collaboration with [Teddy Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teddy_Wilson "Teddy Wilson") produced the hit "[What a Little Moonlight Can Do](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What_a_Little_Moonlight_Can_Do "What a Little Moonlight Can Do")", which became a [jazz standard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_standard "Jazz standard"). Throughout the 1930s and 1940s, Holiday had mainstream success on labels such as [Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records") and [Decca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decca_Records "Decca Records"). However, by the late 1940s, she was beset with legal troubles and drug abuse. After a short prison sentence, Holiday performed a sold-out concert at [Carnegie Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Hall "Carnegie Hall"). She was a successful concert performer throughout the 1950s, with two further sold-out shows at Carnegie Hall. Because of personal struggles and an altered voice, Holiday's final recordings were met with mixed reaction, but were mild commercial successes. Her final album, *Billie Holiday*, was released shortly before her death, in July 1959 and changed to *[Last Recording](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Recording "Last Recording")* after her death. Holiday died of [cirrhosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cirrhosis "Cirrhosis") and heart failure on July 17, 1959, at age 44.

Holiday won four [Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Awards "Grammy Awards"), all of them posthumously, for [Best Historical Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Historical_Album "Grammy Award for Best Historical Album"). She was inducted into the [Grammy Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Hall_of_Fame "Grammy Hall of Fame") and the [National Rhythm & Blues Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rhythm_&_Blues_Hall_of_Fame "National Rhythm & Blues Hall of Fame"). In 2000, Holiday was also inducted into the [Rock and Roll Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_Roll_Hall_of_Fame "Rock and Roll Hall of Fame") as an early influence; their website states that "Billie Holiday changed jazz forever".[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERock_&_Roll_Hall_of_Fame-2) She was named one of the [50 Great Voices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/50_Great_Voices "50 Great Voices") by [NPR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NPR "NPR") and was ranked fourth on the *[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")* list of "200 Greatest Singers of All Time" (2023).[[3]](#cite_note-3) Several films about Holiday's life have been released, including [*Lady Sings the Blues*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady_Sings_the_Blues_(film) "Lady Sings the Blues (film)") (1972) and *[The United States vs. Billie Holiday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_United_States_vs._Billie_Holiday "The United States vs. Billie Holiday")* (2021).

### 1915–1929: Childhood

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Billie_Holiday&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 1915–1929: Childhood")]

Eleanora Fagan[[4]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke,20029-4)[[5]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTE) was born on April 7, 1915,[[6]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTE) in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia") to an [African-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African-American "African-American") unwed teenage couple [Clarence Halliday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarence_Holiday "Clarence Holiday") and Sarah Julia "Sadie" Fagan ([née](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_name#Maiden_and_married_names "Birth name") Harris). Her mother moved to Philadelphia at age 19,[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEO'Meally,199164-7) after being evicted from her parents' home in the [Sandtown-Winchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandtown-Winchester,_Baltimore "Sandtown-Winchester, Baltimore") neighborhood of [Baltimore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore "Baltimore"), Maryland, for becoming pregnant. **Billie Holiday** (born **Eleanora Fagan**; April 7, 1915 – July 17, 1959) was an American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") and [swing music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing_music "Swing music") singer. Nicknamed "**Lady Day**" by her friend and music partner, [Lester Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lester_Young "Lester Young"), Holiday made significant contributions to jazz music and [pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music") singing. Her vocal style, strongly influenced by jazz instrumentalists, inspired a new way of manipulating [phrasing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phrase_(music) "Phrase (music)") and [tempo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tempo "Tempo"). Holiday was known for her vocal delivery and [improvisational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_improvisation "Jazz improvisation") skills.[[1]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOstendorf,_May1993201–202-1)

After a turbulent childhood, Holiday began singing in nightclubs in [Harlem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlem "Harlem") where she was heard by producer [John Hammond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Henry_Hammond "John Henry Hammond"), who liked her voice. Holiday signed a recording contract with [Brunswick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunswick_Records "Brunswick Records") in 1935. Her collaboration with [Teddy Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teddy_Wilson "Teddy Wilson") produced the hit "[What a Little Moonlight Can Do](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What_a_Little_Moonlight_Can_Do "What a Little Moonlight Can Do")", which became a [jazz standard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_standard "Jazz standard"). Throughout the 1930s and 1940s, Holiday had mainstream success on labels such as [Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records") and [Decca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decca_Records "Decca Records"). However, by the late 1940s, she was beset with legal troubles and drug abuse. After a short prison sentence, Holiday performed a sold-out concert at [Carnegie Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Hall "Carnegie Hall"). She was a successful concert performer throughout the 1950s, with two further sold-out shows at Carnegie Hall. Because of personal struggles and an altered voice, Holiday's final recordings were met with mixed reaction, but were mild commercial successes. Her final album, *Billie Holiday*, was released shortly before her death, in July 1959 and changed to *[Last Recording](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Recording "Last Recording")* after her death. Holiday died of [cirrhosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cirrhosis "Cirrhosis") and heart failure on July 17, 1959, at age 44.

Holiday won four [Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Awards "Grammy Awards"), all of them posthumously, for [Best Historical Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Historical_Album "Grammy Award for Best Historical Album"). She was inducted into the [Grammy Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Hall_of_Fame "Grammy Hall of Fame") and the [National Rhythm & Blues Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rhythm_&_Blues_Hall_of_Fame "National Rhythm & Blues Hall of Fame"). In 2000, Holiday was also inducted into the [Rock and Roll Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_Roll_Hall_of_Fame "Rock and Roll Hall of Fame") as an early influence; their website states that "Billie Holiday changed jazz forever".[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERock_&_Roll_Hall_of_Fame-2) She was named one of the [50 Great Voices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/50_Great_Voices "50 Great Voices") by [NPR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NPR "NPR") and was ranked fourth on the *[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")* list of "200 Greatest Singers of All Time" (2023).[[3]](#cite_note-3) Several films about Holiday's life have been released, including [*Lady Sings the Blues*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady_Sings_the_Blues_(film) "Lady Sings the Blues (film)") (1972) and *[The United States vs. Billie Holiday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_United_States_vs._Billie_Holiday "The United States vs. Billie Holiday")* (2021).

Eleanora Fagan[[4]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarke,20029-4)[[5]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTE) was born on April 7, 1915,[[6]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTE) in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia") to an [African-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African-American "African-American") unwed teenage couple [Clarence Halliday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarence_Holiday "Clarence Holiday") and Sarah Julia "Sadie" Fagan ([née](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_name#Maiden_and_married_names "Birth name") Harris). Her mother moved to Philadelphia at age 19,[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEO'Meally,199164-7) after being evicted from her parents' home in the [Sandtown-Winchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandtown-Winchester,_Baltimore "Sandtown-Winchester, Baltimore") neighborhood of [Baltimore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore "Baltimore"), Maryland, for becoming pregnant. Musical artist

"**Mother**" **Maybelle Carter** (born **Maybelle Addington**; May 10, 1909 – October 23, 1978) was an American [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music") musician and "among the first" to use the [Carter scratch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carter_Family_picking "Carter Family picking"),[[1]](#cite_note-1) with which she "helped to turn the guitar into a [lead instrument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead_instrument "Lead instrument")."[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3) It was named after her. She was a member of the original [Carter Family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carter_Family "Carter Family") act from the late 1920s until the early 1940s and a member of the Carter Sisters and Mother Maybelle group.[[4]](#cite_note-Zwonitzer-4)

## Biography

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Maybelle_Carter&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

Maybelle Addington was born on May 10, 1909, in [Nickelsville, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nickelsville,_Virginia "Nickelsville, Virginia"), the daughter of Margaret Elizabeth (née Kilgore; 1879–1960) and Hugh Jackson Addington (1877–1929).[[5]](#cite_note-5)

On March 13, 1926, Maybelle married [Ezra Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ezra_Carter "Ezra Carter"). They had three daughters, [Helen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helen_Carter "Helen Carter"), [June](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/June_Carter_Cash "June Carter Cash"), and [Anita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anita_Carter "Anita Carter").[[4]](#cite_note-Zwonitzer-4)

She was a member of the [Carter Family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carter_Family "Carter Family"), formed in 1927 by her brother-in-law, [A. P. Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A._P._Carter "A. P. Carter"), who was married to her cousin [Sara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sara_Carter "Sara Carter"), also part of the trio. The [Carter Family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carter_Family "Carter Family") was one of the first commercial rural country music groups. Maybelle helped create the group's unique sound with her innovative guitar style, using her thumb to play the melody on the bass strings and her index finger to fill out the rhythm.[[4]](#cite_note-Zwonitzer-4) Her technique, sometimes known as the Carter Scratch, influenced the guitar's shift from rhythm to lead instrument.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

The [Grand Ole Opry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Ole_Opry "Grand Ole Opry") community of the early 1950s widely respected her, regarding her as a matriarchal figure in country music circles and popularly calling her "Mother Maybelle", although she was only in her forties. Maybelle and her daughters toured from the 1940s through the 1960s as "The Carter Sisters and Mother Maybelle", but after the death of A. P. Carter in 1960, the group revived the name "The Carter Family." They frequently toured with [Johnny Cash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Cash "Johnny Cash"), her son‑in‑law, beginning in 1968. The group performed regularly on Cash's weekly network [variety show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Johnny_Cash_Show_(TV_series) "The Johnny Cash Show (TV series)") from 1969 to 1971. She briefly reunited with former Carter Family member Sara Carter during the 1960s folk music revival, with Sara singing lead and Maybelle providing harmony as before, in their 1966 reunion album.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

Carter made occasional solo recordings during the 1960s and 1970s, usually full-length albums. Her final such work, a two-record set released on Columbia Records, appeared on *[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_(magazine) "Billboard (magazine)")'*s best-selling country albums chart in 1973 when she was 64. She was also featured on [The Nitty Gritty Dirt Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nitty_Gritty_Dirt_Band "The Nitty Gritty Dirt Band")'s 1972 recording *[Will the Circle Be Unbroken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Will_the_Circle_be_Unbroken_(Nitty_Gritty_Dirt_Band_album) "Will the Circle be Unbroken (Nitty Gritty Dirt Band album)")*.

Carter died from a [respiratory disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Respiratory_disease "Respiratory disease") on October 23, 1978, at age 69.[[8]](#cite_note-8) She was interred next to her husband, Ezra, in [Hendersonville Memory Gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hendersonville_Memory_Gardens "Hendersonville Memory Gardens") in [Hendersonville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hendersonville,_Tennessee "Hendersonville, Tennessee"), Tennessee. Two of their daughters, Helen and Anita, are buried nearby.[[9]](#cite_note-Carter's_resting_place-9)

## Musicianship

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Maybelle_Carter&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Musicianship")]

### Guitar

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Maybelle_Carter&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Guitar")]

According to statements made by Carter during a transcribed public performance, she began studying guitar at age 13 when she acquired an instrument.[[10]](#cite_note-Carter,_M._1975-10) She was both an early female guitarist with national exposure and one of the first to use the guitar as a lead instrument in country music.[[11]](#cite_note-11)[[12]](#cite_note-Bunch,_W._2009-12)

Writers have identified at least three or four styles played by Maybelle Carter. She often tuned her guitar down, sometimes as many as five frets, but sometimes used a [capo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capo_(musical_device) "Capo (musical device)") to increase the instrument's range.[[10]](#cite_note-Carter,_M._1975-10)[[13]](#cite_note-ReferenceD-13) Her most famous and widely recorded style is sometimes called "the Carter Scratch," or "thumb-lead style." This technique involved playing a melody on the instrument's three bass strings while strumming the three treble strings for rhythm. She used thumb and finger picks while playing.[[14]](#cite_note-14)

Another style, later popularized by other musicians, was essentially the reverse of the thumb-lead style. In this style, Carter fingerpicked a melody on the three treble strings while brushing a rhythm on the bass strings with her thumb. It is often said that she first saw this style played by African American musician [Lesley Riddle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lesley_Riddle "Lesley Riddle"). A third style of Carter's guitar playing involved rapid flatpicking in a country blues rhythm. Her most obscure style was utilized on a few recordings by the Original Carter Family in the 1920s and early 1930s. It may be described as a Hawaiian-influenced slide technique that sometimes sounded like a modern [dobro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dobro "Dobro"). Finally, if other musicians were playing a lead instrument, Maybelle would often strum chords on the guitar to accompany them.[[12]](#cite_note-Bunch,_W._2009-12)[[15]](#cite_note-15)[[16]](#cite_note-ReferenceA-16) Maybelle once filled in for Jimmie Rodgers during a recording session, perfectly mimicking his guitar playing style, in 1932. Rodgers was ill with tuberculosis at that time and had waning stamina during the session.[[17]](#cite_note-Wheeler,_B._E._1976-17)

Carter recorded her signature guitar piece, "Wildwood Flower," on numerous occasions, beginning with the original 1928 version. "The Cannon Ball," recorded with the Original Carter Family in 1930, illustrates Carter's fingerpicking style with thumb/bass fill. Her final recording in the slide guitar style was "My Old Cottage Home" in 1931. "Coal Miner's Blues," recorded for Decca, is an excellent flatpicking illustration.[[18]](#cite_note-Wolfe,_C._2000-18)[[13]](#cite_note-ReferenceD-13)

Guitar recordings she made with the Carter Sisters: "Fourteen Karat Nothing," "I'm Working on a Building," "Take Good Care of Him" — a rapid-tempo re-recording of "Waves on the Sea" — as well as a contemporary-sounding revision of "I'll Be All Smiles Tonight."[[19]](#cite_note-Anonymous,_1980-19)

Solo guitar recordings: "Cumberland Gap," "Victory Rag," "Red Wing," and "Sweet Allie Lee."[[20]](#cite_note-ReferenceB-20)

### Autoharp

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Maybelle_Carter&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Autoharp")]

The autoharp was relatively obscure in the earliest days of recorded country music. The Original Carter Family often used the instrument for rhythm. Still, it was played by Maybelle Carter's cousin and bandmate, Sara Carter, in her intricate style.[[16]](#cite_note-ReferenceA-16) Maybelle Carter is widely credited with the autoharp's popularity and it is still played in country and roots music, .[[21]](#cite_note-21) The autoharp was Maybelle's first instrument. She began tinkering with it as early as the age of four but did not turn a serious focus toward the instrument until around 1940.[[22]](#cite_note-22)

Traditionally the autoharp was strummed as a rhythm instrument.[[23]](#cite_note-Hickey,_N._1971-23) Maybelle developed (alone or perhaps independently of other musicians who did the same) a "pinch and pluck" technique that forms the basis of most modern autoharp playing styles.[[24]](#cite_note-24) This technique allows for playing melodic lead notes on the instrument. Carter's style later evolved to add a fill-in rhythm, similar to her guitar technique. While playing the autoharp, Maybelle would often press cord bars between notes. The effect was a note slurring, a sound similar to a guitar hammer-on. It has been said that pianist Floyd Cramer was especially interested in these embellishments to Maybelle's playing and that they helped to shape his piano technique.[[23]](#cite_note-Hickey,_N._1971-23)[[25]](#cite_note-Carter,_M._1973-25)

As she began to feature the autoharp more and more in concerts and radio work, Carter became frustrated with trying to steady the instrument close enough to a microphone often shared by others. She utilized tables and music stands at first but later got the idea of holding the instrument upside down, across her chest, and playing along what was essentially the head of the harp (nearest the tuning pegs). Before then, musicians played below the cord bars at the opposite end. She discovered this technique allowed more space for her complicated playing style and produced a sweeter tone. During at least one public performance, Maybelle stated that autoharps were manufactured differently to accommodate the playing style she popularized.[[10]](#cite_note-Carter,_M._1975-10)[[23]](#cite_note-Hickey,_N._1971-23)[[26]](#cite_note-Family_Fan_Club_Journal_1994-26)

Maybelle Carter taught at least one workshop on autoharp playing in conjunction with her various appearances at Newport Folk Festivals.[[27]](#cite_note-27) A moderator at the workshop noted that Maybelle should be credited with the first fingerpicked autoharp solo to be captured on commercial recording, referencing "Fair and Tender Ladies" recorded by the Carter Sisters and Mother Maybelle on Columbia Records about 1950.[[28]](#cite_note-Carter,_M._1997-28) She often played the autoharp in that group. Other examples include a simplistic but moving solo she added to "Mountain Lady" on the family's final album before her death. In addition to recordings with the Carter Sisters, which featured her autoharp playing, Maybelle Carter often featured the instrument in her solo work. On her earliest solo album, she offered an old fiddle tune, "Liberty," for the session.[[28]](#cite_note-Carter,_M._1997-28)[[29]](#cite_note-ReferenceC-29) Later, Smash Records issued an album of autoharp solos by Maybelle Carter, which included a few backing musicians and subtle background vocals by the Stephen Scott Singers. "Green Valley Waltz" and "Barbara Allen" were included along with ten other titles. The bulk of her final solo album (from 1973) was composed of autoharp solos in which a whole band of studio musicians accompanied her.[[29]](#cite_note-ReferenceC-29)[[20]](#cite_note-ReferenceB-20)

Mother Maybelle frequently found studio work with other artists to capture the fresh sound she had created. She recorded at least two songs with Johnnie & Jack and at least two with the Wilburn Brothers. The latter collaboration registered a top-ten hit (to which Maybelle Carter was not credited), "Go Away with Me." She also played autoharp on Carl Smith's *Sunday Down South* gospel album. A similar pairing with Flatt & Scruggs led to the *Songs of the Famous Carter Family* album, on which Maybelle contributed mostly through her autoharp playing. In the 1960s, Maybelle helped record an instructional record sold with an autoharp through a mail-order chain store. She contributed a demonstration of the instrument and a small amount of dialogue.[[20]](#cite_note-ReferenceB-20)[[29]](#cite_note-ReferenceC-29)

Musical artist

"**Mother**" **Maybelle Carter** (born **Maybelle Addington**; May 10, 1909 – October 23, 1978) was an American [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music") musician and "among the first" to use the [Carter scratch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carter_Family_picking "Carter Family picking"),[[1]](#cite_note-1) with which she "helped to turn the guitar into a [lead instrument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead_instrument "Lead instrument")."[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3) It was named after her. She was a member of the original [Carter Family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carter_Family "Carter Family") act from the late 1920s until the early 1940s and a member of the Carter Sisters and Mother Maybelle group.[[4]](#cite_note-Zwonitzer-4)

## Biography

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Maybelle_Carter&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

Maybelle Addington was born on May 10, 1909, in [Nickelsville, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nickelsville,_Virginia "Nickelsville, Virginia"), the daughter of Margaret Elizabeth (née Kilgore; 1879–1960) and Hugh Jackson Addington (1877–1929).[[5]](#cite_note-5)

On March 13, 1926, Maybelle married [Ezra Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ezra_Carter "Ezra Carter"). They had three daughters, [Helen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helen_Carter "Helen Carter"), [June](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/June_Carter_Cash "June Carter Cash"), and [Anita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anita_Carter "Anita Carter").[[4]](#cite_note-Zwonitzer-4)

She was a member of the [Carter Family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carter_Family "Carter Family"), formed in 1927 by her brother-in-law, [A. P. Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A._P._Carter "A. P. Carter"), who was married to her cousin [Sara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sara_Carter "Sara Carter"), also part of the trio. The [Carter Family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carter_Family "Carter Family") was one of the first commercial rural country music groups. Maybelle helped create the group's unique sound with her innovative guitar style, using her thumb to play the melody on the bass strings and her index finger to fill out the rhythm.[[4]](#cite_note-Zwonitzer-4) Her technique, sometimes known as the Carter Scratch, influenced the guitar's shift from rhythm to lead instrument.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

The [Grand Ole Opry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Ole_Opry "Grand Ole Opry") community of the early 1950s widely respected her, regarding her as a matriarchal figure in country music circles and popularly calling her "Mother Maybelle", although she was only in her forties. Maybelle and her daughters toured from the 1940s through the 1960s as "The Carter Sisters and Mother Maybelle", but after the death of A. P. Carter in 1960, the group revived the name "The Carter Family." They frequently toured with [Johnny Cash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Cash "Johnny Cash"), her son‑in‑law, beginning in 1968. The group performed regularly on Cash's weekly network [variety show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Johnny_Cash_Show_(TV_series) "The Johnny Cash Show (TV series)") from 1969 to 1971. She briefly reunited with former Carter Family member Sara Carter during the 1960s folk music revival, with Sara singing lead and Maybelle providing harmony as before, in their 1966 reunion album.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

Carter made occasional solo recordings during the 1960s and 1970s, usually full-length albums. Her final such work, a two-record set released on Columbia Records, appeared on *[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_(magazine) "Billboard (magazine)")'*s best-selling country albums chart in 1973 when she was 64. She was also featured on [The Nitty Gritty Dirt Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nitty_Gritty_Dirt_Band "The Nitty Gritty Dirt Band")'s 1972 recording *[Will the Circle Be Unbroken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Will_the_Circle_be_Unbroken_(Nitty_Gritty_Dirt_Band_album) "Will the Circle be Unbroken (Nitty Gritty Dirt Band album)")*.

Carter died from a [respiratory disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Respiratory_disease "Respiratory disease") on October 23, 1978, at age 69.[[8]](#cite_note-8) She was interred next to her husband, Ezra, in [Hendersonville Memory Gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hendersonville_Memory_Gardens "Hendersonville Memory Gardens") in [Hendersonville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hendersonville,_Tennessee "Hendersonville, Tennessee"), Tennessee. Two of their daughters, Helen and Anita, are buried nearby.[[9]](#cite_note-Carter's_resting_place-9)

"Coal Miner's Blues," recorded for Decca, is an excellent flatpicking illustration.[[18]](#cite_note-Wolfe,_C._2000-18)[[13]](#cite_note-ReferenceD-13)

Guitar recordings she made with the Carter Sisters: "Fourteen Karat Nothing," "I'm Working on a Building," "Take Good Care of Him" — a rapid-tempo re-recording of "Waves on the Sea" — as well as a contemporary-sounding revision of "I'll Be All Smiles Tonight."[[19]](#cite_note-Anonymous,_1980-19)

Solo guitar recordings: "Cumberland Gap," "Victory Rag," "Red Wing," and "Sweet Allie Lee."[[20]](#cite_note-ReferenceB-20)

### Autoharp

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Maybelle_Carter&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Autoharp")]

The autoharp was relatively obscure in the earliest days of recorded country music. The Original Carter Family often used the instrument for rhythm. Still, it was played by Maybelle Carter's cousin and bandmate, Sara Carter, in her intricate style.[[16]](#cite_note-ReferenceA-16) Maybelle Carter is widely credited with the autoharp's popularity and it is still played in country and roots music, .[[21]](#cite_note-21) The autoharp was Maybelle's first instrument. She began tinkering with it as early as the age of four but did not turn a serious focus toward the instrument until around 1940.[[22]](#cite_note-22)

Traditionally the autoharp was strummed as a rhythm instrument.[[23]](#cite_note-Hickey,_N._1971-23) Maybelle developed (alone or perhaps independently of other musicians who did the same) a "pinch and pluck" technique that forms the basis of most modern autoharp playing styles.[[24]](#cite_note-24) This technique allows for playing melodic lead notes on the instrument. Carter's style later evolved to add a fill-in rhythm, similar to her guitar technique. While playing the autoharp, Maybelle would often press cord bars between notes. The effect was a note slurring, a sound similar to a guitar hammer-on. It has been said that pianist Floyd Cramer was especially interested in these embellishments to Maybelle's playing and that they helped to shape his piano technique.[[23]](#cite_note-Hickey,_N._1971-23)[[25]](#cite_note-Carter,_M._1973-25)

As she began to feature the autoharp more and more in concerts and radio work, Carter became frustrated with trying to steady the instrument close enough to a microphone often shared by others. She utilized tables and music stands at first but later got the idea of holding the instrument upside down, across her chest, and playing along what was essentially the head of the harp (nearest the tuning pegs). Before then, musicians played below the cord bars at the opposite end. She discovered this technique allowed more space for her complicated playing style and produced a sweeter tone. During at least one public performance, Maybelle stated that autoharps were manufactured differently to accommodate the playing style she popularized.[[10]](#cite_note-Carter,_M._1975-10)[[23]](#cite_note-Hickey,_N._1971-23)[[26]](#cite_note-Family_Fan_Club_Journal_1994-26)

Maybelle Carter taught at least one workshop on autoharp playing in conjunction with her various appearances at Newport Folk Festivals.[[27]](#cite_note-27) A moderator at the workshop noted that Maybelle should be credited with the first fingerpicked autoharp solo to be captured on commercial recording, referencing "Fair and Tender Ladies" recorded by the Carter Sisters and Mother Maybelle on Columbia Records about 1950.[[28]](#cite_note-Carter,_M._1997-28) She often played the autoharp in that group. Other examples include a simplistic but moving solo she added to "Mountain Lady" on the family's final album before her death. In addition to recordings with the Carter Sisters, which featured her autoharp playing, Maybelle Carter often featured the instrument in her solo work. On her earliest solo album, she offered an old fiddle tune, "Liberty," for the session.[[28]](#cite_note-Carter,_M._1997-28)[[29]](#cite_note-ReferenceC-29) Later, Smash Records issued an album of autoharp solos by Maybelle Carter, which included a few backing musicians and subtle background vocals by the Stephen Scott Singers. "Green Valley Waltz" and "Barbara Allen" were included along with ten other titles. The bulk of her final solo album (from 1973) was composed of autoharp solos in which a whole band of studio musicians accompanied her.[[29]](#cite_note-ReferenceC-29)[[20]](#cite_note-ReferenceB-20)

Mother Maybelle frequently found studio work with other artists to capture the fresh sound she had created. She recorded at least two songs with Johnnie & Jack and at least two with the Wilburn Brothers. The latter collaboration registered a top-ten hit (to which Maybelle Carter was not credited), "Go Away with Me." She also played autoharp on Carl Smith's *Sunday Down South* gospel album. A similar pairing with Flatt & Scruggs led to the *Songs of the Famous Carter Family* album, on which Maybelle contributed mostly through her autoharp playing. In the 1960s, Maybelle helped record an instructional record sold with an autoharp through a mail-order chain store. She contributed a demonstration of the instrument and a small amount of dialogue.[[20]](#cite_note-ReferenceB-20)[[29]](#cite_note-ReferenceC-29)

Musical artist

**Bessie Smith** (April 15, 1892 – September 26, 1937) was an American [blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues "Blues") singer widely renowned during the [Jazz Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Age "Jazz Age"). Nicknamed the "[Empress of the Blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honorific_nicknames_in_popular_music "Honorific nicknames in popular music")" and formerly Queen of the Blues, she was the most popular female blues singer of the 1930s. Inducted into the [Rock and Roll Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_Roll_Hall_of_Fame "Rock and Roll Hall of Fame") in 1989, she is often regarded as one of the greatest singers of her era and was a major influence on fellow [blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues "Blues") singers, as well as [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") vocalists.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bessie_Smith#cite_note-1)

Born in [Chattanooga, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chattanooga,_Tennessee "Chattanooga, Tennessee"), Smith was young when her parents died, and she and her six siblings survived by performing on street corners. She began touring and performed in a group that included [Ma Rainey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ma_Rainey "Ma Rainey"), and then went out on her own. Her successful recording career with [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records") began in 1923, but her performing career was cut short by a car crash that killed her at the age of 45.

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bessie_Smith&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

### Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bessie_Smith&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early life")]

[![Image 5: Portrait of Bessie Smith, 1936](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/79/BessieSmith.jpg/330px-BessieSmith.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BessieSmith.jpg)

Smith in 1936

The 1900 census indicates that her family reported that Bessie Smith was born in [Chattanooga, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chattanooga,_Tennessee "Chattanooga, Tennessee"), in July 1892.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bessie_Smith#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bessie_Smith#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bessie_Smith#cite_note-4) The 1910 census gives her age as 16,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bessie_Smith#cite_note-5) and a birth date of April 15, 1894, which appears on subsequent documents and was observed as her birthday by the Smith family. The 1870 and 1880 censuses report several older siblings or half-siblings.

Smith was the daughter of Laura and William Smith, a laborer and part-time [Baptist preacher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_church "Black church") (he was listed in the 1870 census as a "minister of the [gospel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel "Gospel")", in [Moulton, Lawrence County, Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moulton,_Alabama "Moulton, Alabama")). He died while his daughter was too young to remember him. By the time Bessie was nine, her mother and a brother had also died and her older sister Viola took charge of caring for her siblings. As a consequence, Bessie was unable to gain an education.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bessie_Smith#cite_note-Albertson2003-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bessie_Smith#cite_note-7)

Due to her parents' death and her poverty, Bessie experienced a "wretched childhood."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bessie_Smith#cite_note-Moore_1969-8) To earn money for their impoverished household, Bessie and her brother Andrew [busked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Busking "Busking") on the streets of [Chattanooga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chattanooga "Chattanooga"). She sang and danced as he played the [guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar "Guitar"). They often performed on "street corners for pennies,"[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bessie_Smith#cite_note-Moore_1969-8) and their habitual location was in front of the White Elephant Saloon at Thirteenth and Elm streets, in the heart of the city's African-American community.

In 1904, her oldest brother Clarence left home and joined a small traveling troupe owned by Moses Stokes. "If Bessie had been old enough, she would have gone with him," said Clarence's widow, Maud. "That's why he left without telling her, but Clarence told me she was ready, even then. Of course, she was only a child."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bessie_Smith#cite_note-9)

In 1912, Clarence returned to Chattanooga with the Stokes troupe and arranged an audition for his sister with the troupe managers, Lonnie and Cora Fisher. Bessie was hired as a dancer rather than a vocalist since the company already included popular singer [Ma Rainey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ma_Rainey "Ma Rainey").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bessie_Smith#cite_note-Moore_1969-8) Contemporary accounts indicate that, while Ma Rainey did not teach Smith to sing, she likely helped her develop a stage presence.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bessie_Smith#cite_note-10) Smith eventually moved on to performing in [chorus lines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chorus_line "Chorus line"), making the "81" Theatre
